name: Archetype: guerrilla and insurgent forces

weightNotes.aggression: Mao, On Guerrilla Warfare: attack only where and when the enemy is weak and avoid battles that cannot be won; FM 3-24 (2006) describes protracted struggle designed to weaken government control rather than seek decisive battle. Low.
weightNotes.maneuver: Pure manoeuvre in the sense of avoiding attrition: disperse, strike, vanish (Jalali and Grau, The Other Side of the Mountain, on mujahideen raids and ambushes). High.
weightNotes.flanking: Ambushes on columns and lines of communication, attacks on flanks and rear rather than fronts; the dominant mujahideen and Viet Cong tactic. High.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Insurgents rarely hold or besiege cities; they operate from rural terrain (RAND How Insurgencies End: insurgencies suited to rural terrain). Exceptions (ISIS Mosul 2014-17) ended badly for the insurgent. Very low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Small bands commit what they have to a raid; the 'reserve' is the population and sanctuary, not a held-back force. Low.
weightNotes.scouting: FM 3-24: insurgents draw intelligence from the population they live among; local knowledge and informants see the counterinsurgent's moves. High, though without technical ISR.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Doctrine is to break contact early and preserve the force (Mao's sixteen-character formula opens 'the enemy advances, we retreat'). Lowest of all profiles; well below breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Light infantry with small arms, RPGs, mortars, IEDs; no armour or air. Very low.
weightNotes.initiative: Cells and bands act on local judgement under loose political direction; decentralisation is forced by dispersion (Jalali and Grau). High, though coordination between groups is poor.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: RAND How Insurgencies End: 'sanctuary is vital to insurgents' and withdrawal of state sponsorship typically leads to defeat; operations stay near base areas, caches and borders. Middling-high.

summary: Irregular forces fighting a protracted war against a stronger state or occupier: Viet Cong, Afghan mujahideen, Iraqi insurgents 2003-11, the Taliban, many African and Latin American movements. They avoid pitched battle, disperse among the population, ambush convoys and patrols, use IEDs, raids and terrorism, and fall back to rural or cross-border sanctuaries. Mao's three phases (strategic defence, stalemate, counteroffensive) describe the ideal path from guerrilla war to regular war.
whyItWorked: Protracted conflict favours the insurgent (FM 3-24): the stronger side cannot find a decisive target and its political will erodes. RAND's study of 89 insurgencies finds they last about ten years on average. Mujahideen with outside sponsorship and Pakistani sanctuary forced the Soviet withdrawal in 1989; Iraqi insurgents and the Taliban outlasted the US (Iraq 2011, Afghanistan 2021).
whereItFailed: When sanctuary and sponsorship are removed or the insurgent tries to hold ground: RAND finds withdrawal of state sponsorship typically leads to defeat and terrorism often backfires. ISIS lost its cities (Mosul, Raqqa 2017) once it fought conventionally; the Tamil Tigers were destroyed in 2009 after shifting to conventional defence; the Viet Cong were gutted in the 1968 Tet Offensive when they massed in the open.

sources.title: Mao Tse-tung, On Guerrilla Warfare (1937), Marxists Internet Archive
Connable and Libicki, How Insurgencies End (RAND MG-965, 2010)
Jalali and Grau, The Other Side of the Mountain: Mujahideen Tactics in the Soviet-Afghan War, Internet Archive
Rayburn and Sobchak, The U.S. Army in the Iraq War, Vol. 1 (US Army War College Press, 2019)
